headline: Parliamentary Clerk Begins Disqualification Hearings After Rebel MP Fails To Properly Align His Desk Stationery
body:
Q: Mr. Chatterjee, you have served as a Clerk of the House for three decades, but these new disqualification notices for the 20 rebel MPs seem… unusually focused on office supplies. Is this standard procedure?

A: It is entirely standard. The Speaker’s office has always held that legislative integrity begins with the presentation of one’s desk. We simply couldn't ignore the fact that the Member from Sector 7 had his stapler oriented at a 45-degree angle, which is a clear violation of the ‘Uniformity of Parliamentary Workspace’ guidelines.

Q: But isn't disqualification a bit steep for a tilted stapler? The MPs claim they were simply repositioning it to reach a loose pile of reports.

A: That is exactly the kind of excuse we hear from dissenters. If we allow for a ‘repositioning’ defense, next we’ll have members using colorful sticky notes instead of the approved beige ones. Disqualification isn't just about party loyalty; it’s about maintaining a rigid aesthetic standard in the legislative chambers. If your paperclips aren't sorted by gauge, are you truly serving the people?

Q: The rebel MPs have argued that the party is using these procedural audits to purge members who disagreed with the recent caucus vote. What do you say to that?

A: I wouldn't know anything about caucus votes, but I do know that there were three distinct blue ballpoint pens on the desk of an MP who belongs to a party that strictly mandates black ink. That is a betrayal of the House’s visual decorum, and in my book, that’s grounds for a permanent exit from the floor.
caption: Desk aesthetics are the bedrock of democracy. Why settle for policy debates when you can audit the pen color of your political rivals? #ParliamentaryDiscipline #DeskAudit #BureaucracyWins (satire)
igHook: Would you lose your job if your manager inspected the angle of your stapler?

judgeVerdict.reasoning: Candidate 12 (Stationery Alignment) stands out for its specific, absurdly petty bureaucratic logic—the idea that disqualification is a matter of 'visual decorum'—which feels much fresher than the 'game show' or 'lost mail' tropes present in other entries. While Candidate 4 was a strong, warm runner-up, Candidate 12’s sharp focus on the specific absurdity of desk-alignment provides a more vivid and hilarious image that perfectly satirizes institutional pedantry.
